Lattice sidecar (vendor) 0.4 ms x 5 = 2 ms, but measured with mTLS off. Lattice node-proxy 0.9 ms x 5 = 4.5 ms, plus edge (e.g. 0.8 ms if Portcullis is the edge, about 5.3 ms), within 10 ms. evidence.claim: go-spiffe v2 is a Go library that uses the SPIFFE Workload API to set up mTLS between workloads (spiffetls.Listen / spiffetls.Dial with tlsconfig authorizers). It requires a running SPIRE deployment (or another Workload API implementation) and the SPIFFE_ENDPOINT_SOCKET address.

The cost is changing code in all 14 services plus running SPIRE, which is a real burden for 3 engineers (C4) and a timeline risk (C5).

evidence.claim: For comonotonic (perfectly positively rank-correlated) random variables, quantiles are exactly additive: the alpha-percentile of the sum equals the sum of the alpha-percentiles. Comonotonicity gives no diversification benefit, and it cannot produce superadditivity.
evidence.applicability: D1: if every checkout hop were slow at the same time (fully correlated, e.g. one shared bottleneck driving all hops), the end-to-end p99 would equal the sum of the per-hop p99s. So the summed figure in E7 is exact in that limiting case.
evidence.limitations: Search-result snippets only. A WebFetch of aggregate.readthedocs.io and ar.casact.org failed (host not resolvable in this session). These are general probability and risk-measure sources, not latency-specific ones. Real hops are only partially correlated.

evidence.claim: Quantiles (VaR) are not subadditive in general: the quantile of a sum can exceed the sum of the quantiles, even for independent variables. The classic Embrechts et al. example uses two independent Pareto variables with P(Xi > x) = x^(-1/2), x >= 1 (infinite mean). For these the quantile of the sum exceeds the sum of the quantiles at every level alpha in (0,1). For Pareto-type tails with index beta, the limiting ratio of the VaR of the sum to the sum of the VaRs is n^(1/beta - 1), which is above 1 when beta < 1. Superadditivity can also arise with discrete or mixed distributions.
evidence.applicability: D1: a sum of per-hop p99s is not a guaranteed upper bound on the end-to-end p99, even when hops are independent. Whether it over- or under-states depends on the shape of each hop's delay distribution in its tail.
evidence.limitations: Search-result snippets only, not fetched (ar.casact.org could not be resolved). The cleanest counterexamples use infinite-mean distributions, which real proxy latency does not have. The latency-relevant mechanism (rare large spikes) is my own inference in E18. The original 2002 Embrechts text was not retrieved; it is cited through secondary sources.

evidence.claim: Danielsson et al. show that VaR is subadditive in the relevant tail region for multivariate regularly varying (fat-tailed but finite-mean) returns, and that it is subadditive for all log-concave distributions. They argue subadditivity violations are not a practical concern for typical fat-tailed data. In that regime, the quantile of a sum of independent terms is at or below the sum of their quantiles (a diversification benefit).

source.title: Danielsson, de Vries, Jorgensen, Samorodnitsky, Mandira - subadditivity of VaR

evidence.applicability: D1: if per-hop added latency is roughly independent across hops and well-behaved in the tail (log-concave or smooth, finite-mean tails), the summed p99 in E7 overestimates the end-to-end p99. In that case it is a conservative estimate.

evidence.claim: Synthesis on how per-hop p99s combine across sequential hops. (a) Fully correlated (comonotonic) hops: the end-to-end p99 equals the sum of the per-hop p99s (E13). (b) Independent hops with smooth, light or moderate tails: the end-to-end p99 is usually below the sum, so the sum is conservative (E15). (c) Independent hops whose delay has rare large spikes with per-hop probability below 1%: the spikes do not appear in any per-hop p99, but they compound across hops (1-(1-p)^n), so the end-to-end p99 can be far above the sum (E9, E14, E16). Illustrative example, not from any source: each hop takes 0.5 ms with probability 0.995 and 20 ms with probability 0.005. Per-hop p99 = 0.5 ms, so the sum over 5 hops = 2.5 ms. But P(at least one spike in 5 independent hops) = 1 - 0.995^5, about 2.5%, which is more than 1%, so the end-to-end p99 is at least 20 ms. (d) Partial correlation, which is likely for node-proxy mode where co-located hops share one proxy, or with shared CPU, GC or network, falls between these cases. Conclusion: the summed p99 is not a guaranteed conservative upper estimate. It is conservative only when the per-hop tails are well-behaved.
evidence.applicability: Directly addresses D1. Sidecar mode: 2.6 ms x 5 already exceeds 10 ms. Since sums are usually conservative under well-behaved tails, a true end-to-end p99 could be lower, so 'fails R3' is likely but not proven. Node-proxy mode: about 5.3 ms passes on the sum, but a tail-spike regime could push the true end-to-end p99 higher, so 'passes R3' is also not proven. Both conclusions need an end-to-end p99 measurement of the full edge plus checkout chain.
evidence.limitations: My own reasoning, with an invented numerical example used only to show the mechanism. No per-hop latency histograms are available in the fixtures, so the regime that applies to Lattice is unknown. 'Added p99 per hop' in E5 is presumably a difference of p99s, not the p99 of the added delay, which makes the summation even less well-founded.
